status.notice: This is scaffolding, not the essay. Every chapter, scene, line, and illustration here is a structural stand-in used to build and check the website before the writing is wired in. Nothing below states a position held by TJ, Koj, or Vier, and no friend shown here is a real person. The sources are the real audited ones, and each shows how far it was actually checked.

project.title: What Does It Take to Be Happy?
project.question: What does it take to be happy?
project.summary: Happiness takes different forms. Small joys count, while security, time, relationships, and freedom shape who can sustain them. This is a working synthesis, not a formula that predicts feelings or erases disagreements.

sources.label: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I
sources.intendedRole: Flourishing across a life, activity, virtue, and external goods.
sources.limitation: This is a translation, not the Greek, and Book I is one part of the work. That external goods matter is Aristotle's claim; the further question of who is in a position to obtain them is the group's, not his.
sources.evidenceBasis: Full text read at The Internet Classics Archive on 9 October 2026; Book I, Chapters 7 and 8.
sources.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, W. D. Ross translation, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT).
sources.supportedClaim: Aristotle's account locates the human good in virtuous activity across a complete life rather than in a pleasant moment, and his own text states that external goods and equipment are needed for it.

sources.label: Kahneman & Deaton (2010)
sources.intendedRole: Everyday emotional well-being versus life evaluation and income patterns.
sources.limitation: US respondents, 2008–2009, self-reported and correlational. The plateau figure is a value in that dataset in US dollars of that period; it cannot be converted into a peso figure or a national standard.
sources.evidenceBasis: The publisher page returned HTTP 403 on 9 October 2026. The full text was read from the August 2010 author copy, and the published abstract was retrieved separately through NCBI E-utilities and matched it word for word.
sources.citation: Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton, "High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being", Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107(38), 2010, pp. 16489–16493. doi:10.1073/pnas.1011492107.
sources.supportedClaim: Everyday emotional well-being and life evaluation are distinct measures with different correlates, and in this dataset they related to income differently.

sources.label: Palanca-Tan, income and happiness in Koronadal (2021)
sources.intendedRole: Income and happiness in the Koronadal setting.
sources.limitation: One low-income city in Mindanao in 2019, not a national sample. The threshold the paper reports belongs to that sample and is not a Filipino price of happiness. Its highest income band holds only 30 respondents.
sources.evidenceBasis: Journal page read and the full PDF downloaded and text-extracted on 9 October 2026; abstract, methods on p. 955, results on p. 956, and Table II.
sources.citation: Rosalina Palanca-Tan, "Income and Happiness: a Philippine Context", Philippine Journal of Science 150(5), October 2021, pp. 951–961.
sources.supportedClaim: In a 2019 household survey of 522 respondents in Koronadal City, mean self-rated happiness was 6.75 on a 0–10 scale despite a poverty incidence above the national figure, and reported happiness rose with income up to roughly PHP 20,000 of monthly household income.

sources.label: r/adultingph discussion of how much money is enough
sources.intendedRole: Where the question of what "enough" means to different people was first encountered.
sources.limitation: Nothing in the essay rests on what this thread contains. Anonymous public posts would remain external accounts rather than evidence even if they had been readable.
sources.evidenceBasis: Not opened. Reddit is unreachable from the working environment used for the audit, and direct requests returned HTTP 403 on 9 October 2026.

sources.label: Lambek (ed.), Ordinary Ethics
sources.intendedRole: Ordinary ethics in everyday speech and action.
sources.limitation: A publisher description is text written about a book, not a passage from it. No sentence of Lambek's own argument was read, so no specific claim is attributed to him.
sources.evidenceBasis: Publisher page read on 9 October 2026. No introduction, chapter, or excerpt is readable there, and no accessible copy of the text was found.
sources.citation: Michael Lambek (ed.), Ordinary Ethics: Anthropology, Language, and Action, Fordham University Press, 2010, 482 pp. ISBN 9780823233168.
sources.supportedClaim: That this edited volume exists, with this editor, publisher, and year, and that its publisher describes its cumulative argument as treating ethics as ordinary and pervasive in speech and action.

sources.label: Sandstrom & Dunn on weak ties
sources.intendedRole: Weak ties and well-being beyond close friends.
sources.limitation: Abstract-level only. These are within-person daily associations, not an experiment showing that adding acquaintances causes happiness, and the abstract states neither sample sizes nor country.
sources.evidenceBasis: Abstract retrieved through NCBI E-utilities for PMID 24769739 on 9 October 2026. The full article was not read.
sources.citation: Gillian M. Sandstrom and Elizabeth W. Dunn, "Social Interactions and Well-Being: The Surprising Power of Weak Ties", Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 40(7), 2014, pp. 910–922. doi:10.1177/0146167214529799.
sources.supportedClaim: On days when people had more interactions with acquaintances and other weak ties, they reported greater happiness and greater feelings of belonging.

sources.label: Galtung, Violence, Peace, and Peace Research
sources.intendedRole: Structural violence and avoidable gaps in realisation.
sources.limitation: The definition turns on what counts as avoidable and on what counts as a potential realisation, which Galtung himself calls highly problematic. That makes it easy to over-apply, so it needs a concrete barrier, named affected people, and a mechanism.
sources.evidenceBasis: The publisher page returned HTTP 403 on 9 October 2026. The full article was read from a scan carrying the published pagination at an alternate host; pp. 168–171.
sources.citation: Johan Galtung, "Violence, Peace, and Peace Research", Journal of Peace Research 6(3), 1969, pp. 167–191. doi:10.1177/002234336900600301.
sources.supportedClaim: Galtung defines violence as the avoidable gap between what people could realise and what they actually realise, and defines structural violence as that gap produced by a social structure with no identifiable actor harming anyone directly.
